SOURCE: "Neural Turing Machines", Alex Graves, Greg Wayne, Ivo Danihelka (Google DeepMind). arXiv:1410.5401v2 [cs.NE], dated 10 Dec 2014. Preprint.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/02-context-engineering/sources/graves-2014-neural-turing-machines.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 26 of 26 pages, 54,424 of 54,424 characters. That includes the experimental-settings tables on pp. 22-23 and the references on pp. 24-26, which I skimmed for origins. The extraction is clean. Plot tick labels come through as stray numbers, but the captions and body text are intact.

CORE CLAIM AND MECHANISM
- Core claim (p.1, abstract): "We extend the capabilities of neural networks by coupling them to external memory resources, which they can interact with by attentional processes. The combined system is analogous to a Turing Machine or Von Neumann architecture but is differentiable end-to-end, allowing it to be efficiently trained with gradient descent."
- Components (p.5): "A Neural Turing Machine (NTM) architecture contains two basic components: a neural network controller and a memory bank." The heads are the controller outputs that parametrise memory reads and writes.
- Differentiability through blurry access (p.5): "We achieved this by defining 'blurry' read and write operations that interact to a greater or lesser degree with all the elements in memory (rather than addressing a single element...)". Focus is sparse, so "the NTM is biased towards storing data without interference."
- Read (p.6): memory M_t is N×M (N locations, each a vector of size M). The read head emits a weighting w_t with sum_i w_t(i)=1 and 0≤w_t(i)≤1. The read vector is r_t = sum_i w_t(i) M_t(i), "a convex combination of the row-vectors".
- Write (p.6): "Taking inspiration from the input and forget gates in LSTM, we decompose each write into two parts: an erase followed by an add." Erase is M~_t(i) = M_{t-1}(i)[1 − w_t(i) e_t]. Add is M_t(i) = M~_t(i) + w_t(i) a_t. Order does not matter across multiple heads.
- Content addressing (p.8): a key k_t and key strength β_t give w^c_t(i) = softmax over i of β_t K[k_t, M_t(i)], where K is cosine similarity. The authors relate this to Hopfield (1982). "retrieval is simple, merely requiring the controller to produce an approximation to a part of the stored data" (p.7).
- Location addressing (pp.7-9): the interpolation gate g_t blends the content weighting with the previous weighting. A shift weighting s_t then rotates it by circular convolution, and γ_t≥1 sharpens it to stop it blurring. The authors call content addressing "strictly more general" but report that "providing location-based addressing as a primitive operation proved essential for some forms of generalisation" (p.7). Three modes (p.9): content-only; content then shift (find a block, then index into it); iterate from the previous weighting.
- Controller choice (pp.9-10): a recurrent controller's hidden state is "akin to the registers in the processor", with memory as RAM. A feedforward controller is more transparent, but "the number of concurrent read and write heads imposes a bottleneck" (p.10).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: An NTM trained on copy sequences of up to length 20 keeps copying at much longer lengths, while LSTM degrades past 20.
  number: train ≤20, test lengths 10/20/30/50/120
  setup: 8-bit random binary vectors, training lengths drawn from 1-20, memory 128×20, no input given during recall
  quote: "NTM continues to copy as the length increases 2, while LSTM rapidly degrades beyond length 20." / "The plots in the bottom row are for a length 120 sequence. The network was only trained on sequences of up to length 20."
  where: p.11; Fig. 4 caption p.12
- claim: Generalisation on copy was capped by memory size, not by the learned algorithm.
  number: 128 locations
  setup: copy task, footnote 2
  quote: "The limiting factor was the size of the memory (128 locations), after which the cyclical shifts wrapped around and previous writes were overwritten."
  where: p.11
- claim: The length-120 copy is not perfect. It has local errors and one global error (a single duplicated vector), which produces a high loss.
  number: none
  setup: Fig. 4
  quote: "The longest one has a few more local errors and one global error ... a single vector is duplicated, pushing all subsequent vectors one step back."
  where: p.12
- claim: On associative recall, NTM reaches near-zero cost in about 30k episodes. LSTM has not reached zero after a million. The feedforward NTM generalises to twice the training length.
  number: ~30,000 episodes; 2-6 items in training; near-perfect up to 12 items; under 1 bit at 15 items
  setup: each item is three 6-bit vectors (18 bits)
  quote: "terminating at near zero cost within approximately 30, 000 episodes, whereas LSTM does not reach zero cost after a million episodes" / "NTM with a feedforward controller is nearly perfect for sequences of up to 12 items (twice the maximum length used in training), and still has an average cost below 1 bit per sequence for sequences of 15 items."
  where: p.15
- claim: The authors read the feedforward NTM learning associative recall faster than the LSTM-controlled NTM as evidence that external memory beats internal state.
  number: none
  quote: "These two results suggest that NTM's external memory is a more effective way of maintaining the data structure than LSTM's internal state."
  where: p.15
- claim: The learned associative-recall algorithm combines content lookup with a location shift. It writes a compressed item representation at each delimiter, then looks up the query and "shifts by one".
  number: none
  quote: "uses a content-based lookup to find the location where it wrote the first representation, and then shifts by one to produce the subsequent item in the sequence"
  where: p.17
- claim: On repeat copy, NTM and LSTM both solve the training range, but only NTM generalises to longer sequences and more repeats. NTM still cannot predict the end marker.
  number: length and repeats each 1-10 in training
  quote: "NTM succeeds with longer sequences and is able to perform more than ten repetitions; however it is unable to keep count of of how many repeats it has completed, and does not predict the end marker correctly."
  where: p.14
- claim: On dynamic N-grams, NTM beats LSTM by a small margin but never reaches the Bayes-optimal estimator.
  number: 6-gram tables, 200-bit sequences, 1000-sequence validation set
  quote: "NTM achieves a small, but significant performance advantage over LSTM, but never quite reaches the optimum cost."
  where: p.19
- claim: On priority sort, NTM substantially outperforms LSTM. The feedforward controller needed 8 heads.
  number: 20 inputs, top 16 output; 8 heads
  quote: "Each input sequence contained 20 binary vectors with corresponding priorities, and each target sequence was the 16 highest-priority vectors in the input." / "eight parallel read and write heads were needed for best performance with a feedforward controller on this task"
  where: pp.19, 21
- claim: Parameter counts. NTM uses far fewer parameters than LSTM, and its parameter count does not grow with the number of memory locations.
  number: copy task: NTM-FF 17,162; NTM-LSTM 67,561; LSTM (3×256) 1,352,969
  quote: "Copy 1 100 128 × 20 10−4 17, 162" (Table 1); "Copy 1 100 128 × 20 10−4 67, 561" (Table 2); "Copy 3× 256 3 × 10−5 1, 352, 969" (Table 3); "This contrasts with NTM, where the number of parameters does not increase with the number of memory locations."
  where: pp.22-23
  The other parameter counts, in the order FF / NTM-LSTM / LSTM: Repeat copy 16,712 / 66,111 / 5,312,007. Associative 146,845 (4 heads, 256 units) / 70,330 / 1,344,518. N-grams 14,656 / 61,749 / 331,905. Priority sort 508,305 (8 heads, 512 units) / 269,038 (5 heads) / 384,424. Memory is 128×20 in every NTM configuration.
- claim: Training setup. All runs use RMSProp with momentum 0.9 and clip gradients elementwise to (-10, 10). All LSTMs have 3 layers. Error is reported in bits per sequence.
  quote: "the RMSProp algorithm was used for training in the form described in (Graves, 2013) with momentum of 0.9" / "all gradient components are clipped elementwise to the range (-10, 10)"
  where: pp.21-22

LIMITS
- The authors call the work preliminary: "This section presents preliminary experiments on a set of simple algorithmic tasks" (p.10). Every task is a small synthetic binary-vector task. There is no natural language and no real-world data.
- There are no tables of final numeric results and no error bars or seed counts. Results are learning curves and qualitative plots of generalisation, and the copy generalisation has no number for its error.
- Conceded failures: the repeat-copy count does not generalise; N-grams fall short of optimal; the length-120 copy has one global error; the LSTM baseline unexpectedly does well on repeat copy, which the authors attribute to a larger network (footnote 3, p.14).
- Memory is fixed at 128×20, and circular shifts wrap and overwrite. The paper does not cover memory allocation, freeing, or scaling memory. Soft addressing touches every location, and the paper does not discuss the compute cost of that.
- Dated: this predates transformers. Its "memory" is a learned differentiable matrix, not retrieval over text. For LLM context engineering the paper works as a conceptual origin of a controller doing attention-based reads and writes to external memory, not as evidence about LLM systems.

BUILDS ON: LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997); differentiable attention (Graves, 2013; Bahdanau et al., 2014); content addressing in Hopfield networks (Hopfield, 1982); RNNs being Turing-complete (Siegelmann and Sontag, 1995); RNN with external stack memory (Das et al., 1992); learning to learn (Hochreiter et al., 2001b); working memory (Baddeley et al., 2009); the gated working-memory model of Hazy et al. (2006); variable binding (Fodor and Pylyshyn, 1988; Smolensky, 1990; Plate, 2003; Kanerva, 2009); Von Neumann (1945); RMSProp as in Graves (2013).

CODE: the learned copy algorithm, which the authors present as pseudocode inferred from memory traces (p.11), verbatim:
initialise: move head to start location / while input delimiter not seen do / receive input vector / write input to head location / increment head location by 1 / end while / return head to start location / while true do / read output vector from head location / emit output / increment head location by 1 / end while

FIGURES
- Best candidate: Figure 2, p.7. "Flow Diagram of the Addressing Mechanism. The key vector, kt, and key strength, βt, are used to perform content-based addressing of the memory matrix, Mt. The resulting content-based weighting is interpolated with the weighting from the previous time step based on the value of the interpolation gate, gt. The shift weighting, st, determines whether and by how much the weighting is rotated. Finally, depending on γt, the weighting is sharpened and used for memory access." It shows the whole content-to-location pipeline in a single picture, where the prose needs Eqs. 5-9.
- Alternative: Figure 1, p.5 (architecture: controller, read/write heads, memory, and the boundary with the outside world). It is the simplest picture of "controller + external memory" for notes/06-memory.md.
- Alternative: Figure 4, p.12 (copy generalisation to length 120 after training only up to length 20).

PROBLEMS: none of substance. The text contains no embedded instructions. Plot axis labels extract as loose numbers, and some equations break across lines (for example Eq. 5), but I reconstructed them from context without needing to guess. Note that the intro (p.10) mentions testing at length 100, while the figures actually show lengths 10/20/30/50/120.
